hypothesis_ledger.title: Socially transmitted graphic and ornamental traditions existed in early Homo sapiens before 70 ka
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: Independent material classes and regions support an early mosaic of display and graphic traditions, while the exact semantic content of those traditions remains partly underdetermined.

hypothesis_ledger.title: Ochre in Middle Stone Age contexts is intrinsically ritual or symbolic
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: Direct functional evidence from ochre retouchers falsifies the single-meaning version of this hypothesis. Ochre must be evaluated artifact-by-artifact and context-by-context.

hypothesis_ledger.title: Early Homo sapiens practiced structured mortuary behavior
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: Qafzeh supports structured mortuary behavior in a specific early Homo sapiens context, but motive and cosmological interpretation remain underdetermined.

hypothesis_ledger.title: Some Middle Paleolithic behaviors crossed Homo population boundaries in the Levant
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: Recent regional synthesis supports substantial behavioral overlap and proposes interaction as a mechanism. Convergence and shared ancestral capacities remain viable alternatives for individual practices.

hypothesis_ledger.title: Blombos and Diepkloof engravings were denotational symbolic signs
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: The selected experimental evidence supports decoration, transmission, style and intentionality but found no clear indication of denotational sign function. Other symbolic functions remain open.

hypothesis_ledger.title: Early symbolic materials were behaviorally multifunctional
hypothesis_ledger.evidence_balance: The direct technological use of ochre, alongside graphic ochre use and personal ornaments in broader Middle Stone Age records, makes a multifunctional model more defensible than assigning one universal meaning to a material category.

synthesis.headline: Early Homo sapiens behavior looks like a mosaic, not a switch flipping on.
findings: Personal ornaments at Bizmoune and deliberate graphic design at Blombos support socially visible and transmitted practices well before 70 ka.
The Blombos/Diepkloof experimental literature supports style, decoration and cultural transmission without demonstrating denotational sign use.
Direct evidence that some ochre pieces served as lithic retouchers makes 'ochre equals ritual' an invalid coding rule.

Qafzeh supports structured early Homo sapiens mortuary behavior while leaving theology and afterlife doctrine underdetermined, paralleling the epistemic boundary already enforced for Neanderthal burials.
Recent Levantine evidence makes strict species-exclusive behavioral narratives harder to sustain, but interaction, convergence and shared ancestry still need to be separated rather than collapsed.
next_tests: Build a cross-pack comparison matrix using identical behavioral constructs for Neanderthals and Homo sapiens.
Separate raw observations such as pigment, perforation, wear, grave position and mark geometry from symbolic/ritual interpretations.
Model first appearances as censored by preservation, excavation intensity and dating uncertainty.
Add object life-history data so multifunctional artifacts are not forced into one ontology slot.
Integrate population-contact evidence before attributing behavioral similarities to transmission, convergence or ancestry.

epistemic_rules: Material category is not behavioral meaning: ochre can be technological, decorative, symbolic, or multifunctional.
Personal ornament is strong evidence of display and social signaling, but the exact encoded meaning may remain unknown.
Graphic design is not automatically denotational writing or language.
Intentional burial is not automatically evidence of an afterlife doctrine or formal religion.
A species label does not make every site, population or practice culturally equivalent.
Behavioral similarity across Homo groups may reflect convergence, shared ancestry, interaction, or combinations of these.
Sparse preservation and excavation histories constrain apparent first appearances.
